extracted.intended_audience: poets, musicians, educators, and founders/guardians responsible for the moral education of youth (readers of Plato's Republic / designers of an ideal-state arts curriculum)
extracted.subtask_short: poetry and music guidelines for guardians
extracted.subtask_description: Normative rules for composing, selecting, and teaching poetry, song, rhythm, melody, instrumentation, and physical training for the guardian class of an ideal state—covering narrative vs imitation, permitted characters, musical modes and rhythms, instruments, and gymnastic/dietary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of narrative (simple narration, imitation, union)
rubrics_metrics.description: All mythology and poetry is a narration of events, either past, present, or to come; narration may be either simple narration, or imitation, or a union of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Homer sometimes speaks in his own person (simple narration) and sometimes takes the person of a character (imitation), e.g., the opening lines of the Iliad where Homer shifts into Chryses' voice. Epic often combines both styles; tragedy and comedy are wholly imitative; dithyramb is an example of the poet-as-only-speaker (simple narration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation by assuming a character's voice and gesture
rubrics_metrics.description: When the poet speaks in the person of another, he assimilates his style to that of the person who is represented; this assimilation by voice or gesture is imitation of the person whose character he assumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically: adopting another's persona requires altering wording, voice, and gesture to create the illusion that the speaker is the character, not the poet; contrast with continuing in the poet's own voice which yields simple narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization: one craft/role per person
rubrics_metrics.description: One man can only do one thing well, and not many; if he attempt many, he will altogether fail of gaining much reputation in any. This is equally true of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for writers/performers: do not attempt to be both tragic and comic (or rhapsodist and actor) with equal excellence; maintain role-consistency appropriate to your function (e.g., a guardian should not adopt multiple, conflicting personae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guardians may imitate only virtuous characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If guardians imitate at all, they should imitate from youth upward only those characters which are suitable to their profession—the courageous, temperate, holy, free, and the like; they should not depict or be skilful at imitating any kind of illiberality or baseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific prohibitions for guardians' imitation: do not allow portrayals or practiced imitation of women quarrelling with husbands, boasting against the gods, in affliction, sorrow, weeping, or in sickness, love, or labour; do not allow depiction/imitation of slaves (male or female) performing slave-offices; do not train guardians to imitate cowards, scolds, mockers, revilers, madmen, or other vicious characters. Rationale: habitual imitation forms character—repeated portrayal of vice breeds vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imitation of trades, animal sounds, and mechanical noises
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians are not to be taught to imitate smiths or other artificers, or oarsmen, or boatswains, nor to imitate the neighing of horses, bellowing of bulls, murmur of rivers, roll of the ocean, thunder, and similar sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: pantomimic or mimicry of such non-moral/lowly matters trains inappropriate habits and distracts from the guardian's single craft of preserving the State; send such performers away rather than allow them to influence guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the pure imitator of virtue; exclude pantomimic/mixed styles for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: The city should admit only the pure imitator of virtue; the pantomimic (the opposite style which imitates anything and is most popular with children and the general public) is unsuitable to the State in which one man plays one part only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although mixed styles are charming and popular, in this political-educational context they are disallowed because they train multiplicity of character rather than the single excellence required of guardians. Pantomimic artists may be honored but must be sent out of the city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple style vs pantomimic style (harmonies and rhythms)
rubrics_metrics.description: One style is simple and has but slight changes (keeping within limits of a single harmony and nearly the same rhythm); the other requires all sorts of harmonies and rhythms because the style has many changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For guardians, choose the simple style (limited harmonies/rhythms) that yields consistency; avoid styles demanding many changes in harmony and rhythm which correspond to the pantomimic approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song/ode components and primacy of words
rubrics_metrics.description: A song or ode has three parts - the words, the melody, and the rhythm; melody and rhythm will depend upon the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: rhythm and harmony are regulated by the words, and not the words by them. Compose words first (with moral content appropriate to guardians), then adapt melody and rhythm to express those words and the temper of the soul represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban harmonies expressive of sorrow and softness; permit Dorian and Phrygian
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmonies expressive of sorrow (mixed or tenor Lydian, full-toned or bass Lydian, and the like) and soft/drinking harmonies (Ionian and Lydian) must be banished; the Dorian and the Phrygian are the warlike and the proper strains to be left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: sorrowful or relaxed harmonies are unfit for guardians (they engender drunkenness, softness, indolence). Keep two strains: the 'strain of necessity' (warlike, crisis/courage) and the 'strain of freedom' (temperance, prudence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit multiplicity of notes/panharmonic scales and complex instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall not maintain artificers of lyres with three corners and complex scales, or makers of any other many-stringed curiously-harmonised instruments; there is no need for a panharmonic scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrument policy: admit only the lyre and the harp for civic use; shepherds may have a pipe in the country. The flute and panharmonic imitators (panharmonic music) are worse than stringed instruments and are to be excluded from the city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythms must be simple and expressive of noble character
rubrics_metrics.description: We ought not to seek out complex systems of metre, or metres of every kind, but rather to discover what rhythms are the expressions of a courageous and harmonious life; adapt the foot and the melody to words having a like spirit, not the words to the foot and melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult musical authorities (e.g., Damon) for which specific metres express which states (meanness, insolence, fury, etc.). Simplicity in rhythm yields grace; complex metres may engender licence or incoherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty, grace, harmony, and good rhythm depend on simplicity of soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of style and harmony and grace and good rhythm depend on simplicity — the true simplicity of a rightly and nobly ordered mind and character, not mere folly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational aim: cultivate a rightly ordered soul in youth so that style, rhythm, and harmony naturally follow; aesthetic qualities mirror moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical training as a formative instrument of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical training is a more potent instrument than any other, because rhythm and harmony find their way into the inward places of the soul and impart grace, making the soul graceful or ungraceful according to its education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: musical education should make youth able to perceive omissions or faults in art and nature, praise the good, hate the bad, and be prepared to welcome reason when it comes. Music cultivates taste and moral disposition before explicit reasoning develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastic training: simple military regimen and plain diet
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnastic, like our simple music, should be simple and especially the military gymnastic; guardians should be trained to be like wakeful dogs—keen of sight and hearing, able to endure many changes of food and water, summer heat and winter cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dietary and regimen rules: prefer soldiers' fare (roast rather than boiled, no sweet sauces, no refined Sicilian or Syracusan delicacies, no Corinthian girls as distractions). Avoid the habits of professional athletes who 'sleep away their lives' and become prone to infirmities; aim for toughness and health suited to campaign conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstain from intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must abstain from intoxication; of all persons a guardian should be the last to get drunk and not know where in the world he is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: a guardian requiring another guardian to assist him when drunk is ridiculous and disqualifying. Temperance is essential to guardians' duty and training.
